title: The marks of a great man
hookLine: the thirty-two marks and the good deeds said to cause them, read as poetry

cards: Look closely at an old statue of the Buddha. A small round mark between the eyebrows. A rounded swelling on the crown of the head.

Sometimes a wheel carved on the sole of each foot. These aren't decorations a sculptor made up. They come from a list of thirty-two marks of a great man, signs that a person will become either a world ruler or a Buddha.
The thirtieth Long Discourse, the Lakkhana Sutta, asks a different question about that list. Not what the marks are. Where they come from.

teach.b: It goes through the marks in groups, and for each it tells what the Buddha did in earlier lives to earn it. Then it repeats the whole thing in verse. A few of them.
The wheels on the soles of his feet: because in past lives he brought happiness to many, took away fear and danger, and gave protection.
Soft, tender hands, with fingers said to be webbed or net-like: because he drew people together in four ways, by giving, by kind words, by helpful action, and by treating people as equals.
Deep blue eyes and lashes like a cow's: because he looked at people kindly, straight and openly, not sideways, not with suspicion.
And the soft white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, the mark you see on statues: because he refused to lie. Read that way, the list stops being strange and becomes a portrait.
A body shaped, over many lives, by what it did. Feet that carried people out of danger. Hands that gave and gathered.
Eyes that looked kindly. A face that told the truth.
Readers take the marks in different ways, as physical signs, as symbols, or as both. The sutta's point holds either way: deeds leave marks.
And there's a kind of marking anyone can see in an ordinary face: the lines of someone who has smiled a lot, the steady eyes of someone who doesn't lie to you.

how: Buddhist images across Asia show some of the thirty-two marks, most visibly the urna between the brows and the ushnisha on the crown, and teachers often explain each mark through the deed the Lakkhana Sutta links to it.

o: a mark or sign, like those of a great man
a fortune read from the lines of the palm
a lucky charm worn to keep harm away

games.q: the marks of a great man: tap the pairs.
p: looking at people straight and kindly

s: the thirty-two marks were invented by later sculptors
they come from an old list in the suttas, and DN 30 explains each one.
DN 30 says the wheels on his soles come from bringing happiness to many
and taking away fear and giving protection.
Buddhists all agree the marks are literal physical features
they have been understood as physical signs, as symbols, or as both.

games.q: the Lakkhana Sutta explains the white tuft between the Buddha's brows. what deed is it said to come from?
games.why: the tuft, the urna, is linked to truthful speech in past lives.

practice: Bring to mind a kind face you know, someone whose kindness shows, and look for where it lives: the eyes, the mouth, the way they tilt their head. Stay with that face for a while.
Then gently feel your own: soften the eyes, let the jaw loosen, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: lakkhana. In DN 30 each of the thirty-two marks is traced to a good deed: kind eyes from looking kindly, the tuft from telling the truth. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali lakkhana: mark, sign, characteristic. the thirty-two mahapurisa-lakkhana, marks of a great man.

carryVoice: Your line: the marks of kindness. Kind eyes come from looking kindly. See you tomorrow.
